notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: omnis closes the phrase ante omnis, so Laocoön is first "before everyone": he stands out from the crowd from the moment he appears.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: magna and caterva are split across the end of the line, so the words spread out like the crowd itself, which shows how many people follow Laocoön.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: used of Androgeos (ii.370) and Dido (iv.136)

notes.label: Laocoön
notes.body: A Trojan priest of Neptune (line 201). Ancient writers disagree about his family; in one version he is the brother of Anchises, Aeneas' father.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: ardens, "blazing", shows Laocoön burning with anger and urgency, so the reader sees how desperate he is to stop the Trojans.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.trans: from the top of the citadel
notes.body: summa and arce are separated by the verb decurrit, so his run down from the heights sits between them, which makes the dash feel long and dramatic.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: The epic equivalent of insanis in Comedy. Virgil has dressed up a phrase that any ordinary Roman might use at seeing something preposterous.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: miseri near the start of the question and cives at its end frame his whole outburst, so the Trojans are called pitiable before they are even named.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Understand esse

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: ulla ends line 43 and dona begins line 44, so "any" hangs at the line end and the reader waits for "gifts": no Greek gift at all can be trusted.

notes.label: Poetic plural
notes.body: dolis is plural where a single trick is meant, which makes the Greeks' deceit sound endless.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated d sound in dona dolis Danaum links gifts, tricks and Greeks together, so the sound itself makes Laocoön's point that Greek gifts are tricks.

notes.label: Rhythm
notes.trans: the line runs quickly on to Danaum
notes.body: The line hurries through dona carere dolis to Danaum, hardly pausing at the caesura, which suits Laocoön's angry, rapid speech.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Ulysses is taken as the Greek schemer par excellence

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: inclusi and Achivi are split by the rest of the line, and the Greeks themselves come last, hidden at the end of the line just as they are hidden inside the horse.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: ‘The Wooden Horse is suspected to be an engine of war, as indeed it was, but the Trojans’ minds were quite pedestrian. They were thinking of the usual siege-tower, from which weapons and blazing fire-brands were thrown into a city’ - Dunlop

notes.label: Interwoven word order
notes.body: haec ... machina and nostros ... muros are interlaced, so the machine and the walls are tangled together in the line, as the horse threatens the city.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: inspectura opens the line, so the idea of the Greeks spying into Trojan homes comes first and sounds sinister.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: ventura follows in the same way as inspectura, which builds up Laocoön's list of the dangers inside the horse.

notes.label: Future participles of purpose
notes.trans: to look into ... to come down
notes.body: inspectura and ventura are future participles expressing purpose, a Greek-style construction, which makes the threat sound as if it is already planned.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: error ends its clause just before the strong pause, so the vague idea of "some trick" is left hanging ominously.

notes.label: Imperative
notes.body: Laocoön gives a direct order, ne credite, which shows how urgent and certain he is.

notes.label: Poetic construction
notes.body: ne with the present imperative is an old, poetic way of saying "do not" (prose would use noli credere), which gives his warning a solemn, prophetic tone.

notes.label: The citadel
notes.body: The arx was the fortified high point of Troy, where Priam's palace and the temples stood. Laocoön runs all the way down from it to the horse on the plain below.

notes.label: Greeks and Trojans
notes.body: Virgil uses several names for the Greeks: Danai (after Danaus, an early king of Argos), Achivi (Achaeans) and Argivi. The Trojans are often Teucri, after Teucer, an early king of Troy.

notes.label: A famous line
notes.trans: I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts
notes.body: One of the most quoted lines in Latin, still used today as a warning to be wary of generosity from an enemy.

questions: Why do you think Virgil makes Laocoön run down from the citadel, with a crowd behind him?
Laocoön offers several explanations for the horse. Which is closest to the truth, and how does his language make him persuasive?
Why do you think the Trojans ignore his warning?

context.body:
Laocoön was a Trojan priest, usually said to be a priest of Apollo, though in this story he is serving Neptune. In Virgil's account he is the only Trojan who sees the danger clearly. Ancient writers told his story in different ways: in some he is punished for an earlier offence against Apollo, but Virgil makes his death look like a punishment for attacking the horse, and that is what persuades the Trojans to take it in.

A famous marble statue of Laocoön and his sons in the coils of the serpents, found in Rome in 1506, is now in the Vatican Museums.
